lesson.title: The Directions a Matrix Cannot Turn

sections.title: Invariant Directions
sections.body:
A matrix $A$ normally does two things to a vector at once: it stretches it and it turns it. An **eigenvector** is a non-zero $v$ on which the turning part simply does not happen, so that $Av$ lands back on the same line through the origin: $$A v = \lambda v, \qquad v \neq 0.$$ The scalar $\lambda$ is the **eigenvalue**, and it records what happened along that line - stretch when $\lambda > 1$, shrink when $0 < \lambda < 1$, flip when $\lambda < 0$, and collapse to the origin when $\lambda = 0$.

Geometrically the eigenvectors are the axes the transformation respects. Off those axes a vector is dragged towards whichever eigendirection has the largest $|\lambda|$, which is why eigenvalues govern the long-run behaviour of anything driven by repeated multiplication.

The exclusion $v \neq 0$ is not fussiness: $A0 = \lambda 0$ holds for every $\lambda$ whatsoever, so admitting $0$ would make every scalar an eigenvalue and destroy the definition. The eigen*value* $0$, by contrast, is perfectly respectable - it says $A$ crushes a whole direction, which is exactly what a singular matrix does.

Notice too that eigenvectors come in lines, never as isolated arrows: if $Av = \lambda v$ then $A(cv) = \lambda(cv)$ for every $c \neq 0$, so a reported eigenvector is only a representative of its line.
sections.code:
A = ( 2  1 )      test three vectors
    ( 1  2 )

  v = (1, 1)     A v = (2*1 + 1*1, 1*1 + 2*1) = (3, 3) = 3 * (1,1)
                 same line, stretched by 3          EIGENVECTOR, lambda = 3

  v = (1, -1)    A v = (2*1 + 1*(-1), 1*1 + 2*(-1)) = (1, -1) = 1 * (1,-1)
                 same line, untouched               EIGENVECTOR, lambda = 1

  v = (1, 0)     A v = (2, 1)
                 (2,1) is not c*(1,0) for any c     NOT an eigenvector

What the transformation does to the whole plane:

        the line through (1,1)      stretched by 3
        the line through (1,-1)     left exactly where it was
        everything else             swung towards the (1,1) line

  Scaling changes nothing:  A(5,5) = (15,15) = 3*(5,5).
  An eigenvector is a LINE, and (1,1) is only its label.

annotations.text: Both coordinates tripled together. That is what 'the output is a scalar multiple of the input' looks like in numbers.
(2,1) points somewhere new, so (1,0) is an ordinary vector. Most vectors are ordinary; the eigendirections are rare.
The eigenvalue equation is homogeneous in v, so any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is another eigenvector with the same eigenvalue.

checkpoint.prompt: With $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, compute each product and answer the last step with `yes` or `no`. Write vectors as `(a,b)` with no spaces.
checkpoint.explain: $A(2,-2) = (2,-2)$ shows the eigenvalue $1$ acting on a rescaled copy of $(1,-1)$: the line, not the particular arrow, is what carries the eigenvalue. $(1,0)$ maps to $(2,1)$, which lies off the horizontal axis, so no scalar $\lambda$ can satisfy $A(1,0) = \lambda(1,0)$ and the vector is not an eigenvector.

sections.title: The Characteristic Polynomial
sections.body:
Rewriting $Av = \lambda v$ as $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$ turns an equation about a mysterious pair $(\lambda, v)$ into a question about a single matrix: for which $\lambda$ does $A - \lambda I$ have a non-zero null vector? A square matrix kills a non-zero vector precisely when it is singular, so the eigenvalues are exactly the roots of $$\det(A - \lambda I) = 0,$$ the **characteristic equation**; its left-hand side is the **characteristic polynomial** $p(\lambda)$.

For an $n \times n$ matrix $p$ has degree $n$ with leading term $(-1)^n\lambda^n$, so such a matrix has at most $n$ eigenvalues, and exactly $n$ when they are counted with multiplicity over $\mathbb{C}$.

In the $2 \times 2$ case the polynomial takes a form worth memorising, $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A$, which gives the two running checks $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \operatorname{tr} A$ and $\lambda_1\lambda_2 = \det A$.

Those identities hold in every dimension - the sum of the eigenvalues is the trace and their product is the determinant - and they catch arithmetic slips far faster than re-solving the polynomial does.
sections.code:
B = ( 4  1 )
    ( 2  3 )

  B - lambda*I = ( 4-lambda      1     )
                 (    2       3-lambda )

  det = (4-lambda)(3-lambda) - (1)(2)
      = 12 - 7*lambda + lambda^2 - 2
      = lambda^2 - 7*lambda + 10
      = (lambda - 5)(lambda - 2)

  eigenvalues:  lambda = 5  and  lambda = 2

Cross-checks, both instant:

  trace B = 4 + 3 = 7        and   5 + 2 = 7    OK
  det B   = 4*3 - 1*2 = 10   and   5 * 2 = 10   OK

The shortcut for any 2x2:

  p(lambda) = lambda^2 - (trace)*lambda + (det)

A triangular matrix needs no work at all - the determinant of a
triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal, so

  ( 1  2  2 )
  ( 0  3  2 )   has p(lambda) = (1-lambda)(3-lambda)(5-lambda),
  ( 0  0  5 )   eigenvalues 1, 3, 5 read straight off the diagonal.

annotations.text: Subtracting lambda*I touches only the diagonal. Subtracting it from every entry is the classic slip and produces a polynomial of the wrong shape.
The coefficient -7 is minus the trace and the constant 10 is the determinant. That pattern is a free check on all your 2x2 work.
The same holds for lower-triangular and diagonal matrices, which is why diagonalising a matrix makes its eigenvalues visible.

checkpoint.prompt: For $C = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & -2 \\ -2 & 9 \end{pmatrix}$, fill in the trace, the determinant and the two eigenvalues. Give plain integers, smaller eigenvalue first.
checkpoint.template:
trace C = ___
det C = ___
lambda_1 = ___
lambda_2 = ___
checkpoint.explain: $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 15\lambda + 50 = (\lambda-5)(\lambda-10)$, and the checks confirm it: $5 + 10 = 15 = \operatorname{tr} C$ and $5 \times 10 = 50 = \det C$. The determinant is $6 \times 9 - (-2)(-2) = 54 - 4 = 50$; forgetting that the product of the two off-diagonal entries is positive here is the usual route to the wrong polynomial.

sections.title: Eigenspaces and Two Kinds of Multiplicity
sections.body:
Once $\lambda$ is known the eigenvectors are found by solving the homogeneous system $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$, so the eigenvectors for $\lambda$, together with $0$, form the null space of $A - \lambda I$. That subspace is the **eigenspace** $E_\lambda$, and calling it a space is the useful part: eigenvectors for one eigenvalue can be added and scaled freely without leaving the set.

An eigenvalue therefore carries two counts. Its **algebraic multiplicity** is its multiplicity as a root of $p(\lambda)$; its **geometric multiplicity** is $\dim E_\lambda = n - \operatorname{rank}(A - \lambda I)$.

They need not agree. The inequality $1 \le \text{geometric} \le \text{algebraic}$ always holds, and an eigenvalue whose geometric multiplicity falls strictly below its algebraic multiplicity is called **defective** - the polynomial promised more independent directions than the null space can supply.

A shear is the standard offender: it repeats an eigenvalue while fixing only a single line, and no amount of algebra can conjure a second independent eigenvector out of a rank that refuses to drop.
sections.code:
DEFECTIVE.   S = ( 1  1 )       p(lambda) = (1-lambda)^2
                 ( 0  1 )       lambda = 1, algebraic multiplicity 2

  S - 1*I = ( 0  1 )   rank 1   =>  dim E_1 = 2 - 1 = 1
            ( 0  0 )

  E_1 = span{ (1,0) }   geometric 1 < algebraic 2   DEFECTIVE
  Geometry: the shear pins the x-axis and slides every other line.

HEALTHY REPEAT.   M = (  5  -1  -1 )   p(lambda) = -(lambda-6)(lambda-4)^2
                      (  0   4   0 )   lambda = 4 has algebraic 2
                      ( -1   1   5 )

  M - 4I = (  1  -1  -1 )   rank 1  =>  dim E_4 = 3 - 1 = 2
           (  0   0   0 )
           ( -1   1   1 )

  E_4 = span{ (1,1,0), (1,0,1) }   geometric 2 = algebraic 2   FINE
  E_6 = span{ (-1,0,1) }           geometric 1 = algebraic 1

So a repeated eigenvalue is not itself the problem.  The question is
always how much rank A - lambda*I actually loses:

  1 <= geometric <= algebraic,  and equality everywhere is what matters.

annotations.text: S - I has one non-zero row, so its rank is 1 and its null space is one-dimensional. Rank is the whole story for the geometric count.
The three rows of M - 4I are multiples of one another, so rank 1 and a two-dimensional eigenplane. Every vector in that plane is scaled by 4.
Geometric multiplicity is at least 1 because lambda being a root forces A - lambda*I singular, hence some non-zero null vector exists.

checkpoint.prompt: Let $N = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. State the characteristic polynomial, give the algebraic and geometric multiplicity of $\lambda = 2$, and say what the rank of $N - 2I$ has to do with your answer.
checkpoint.answer: p(lambda) = -(lambda-2)^2(lambda-3); lambda = 2 has algebraic multiplicity 2 and geometric multiplicity 1, since rank(N - 2I) = 2 gives dim E_2 = 3 - 2 = 1; E_2 = span{(1,0,0)}.
checkpoint.explain: $N$ is triangular, so $p(\lambda) = (2-\lambda)^2(3-\lambda)$ and $\lambda = 2$ is a double root. But $N - 2I$ has the two independent rows $(0,1,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$, so its rank is $2$ and the null space is only $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,0)\}$: geometric $1$ against algebraic $2$, a defect of one. The tempting error is to read the repeated root as a promise of a two-dimensional eigenspace, but only the rank of $N - \lambda I$ can deliver that.

sections.title: Diagonalisation and the Payoff in Powers
sections.body:
Suppose an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors. Place them as the columns of $P$ and the matching eigenvalues down the diagonal of $D$; then $AP = PD$, and since independent columns make $P$ invertible we may write $$A = PDP^{-1}, \qquad D = P^{-1}AP.$$ This is **diagonalisation**, and it says the confusing matrix $A$ is really the simple matrix $D$ seen through a change of basis: $P^{-1}$ rewrites a vector in eigencoordinates, $D$ scales each coordinate independently, and $P$ translates back.

A matrix is diagonalisable exactly when every eigenvalue has geometric multiplicity equal to its algebraic multiplicity, which is another way of saying the eigenvectors span the whole space. Having $n$ distinct eigenvalues is a convenient sufficient condition, never a necessary one.

The payoff arrives with powers. Since the inner factors cancel in pairs, $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$, and $D^k$ costs only $n$ scalar powers, so a $k$-step evolution becomes one formula rather than $k$ matrix multiplications.

That formula is also why eigenvalues predict long-run behaviour: as $k$ grows, $\lambda^k$ for the largest $|\lambda|$ swamps the rest, so the state lines up with its eigenvector - decaying when every $|\lambda| < 1$, settling when the largest is exactly $1$.
sections.code:
A = ( 2  1 )     eigenpairs:  3 with (1,1),   1 with (1,-1)
    ( 1  2 )

  P = ( 1   1 )     D = ( 3  0 )     P^-1 = ( 1/2   1/2 )
      ( 1  -1 )         ( 0  1 )            ( 1/2  -1/2 )

  Multiplying P D P^-1 out returns A exactly.

Powers, because the middles cancel:

  A^k = (P D P^-1)(P D P^-1)...(P D P^-1) = P D^k P^-1

  A^k = ( (3^k + 1)/2   (3^k - 1)/2 )
        ( (3^k - 1)/2   (3^k + 1)/2 )

  k = 5:   3^5 = 243   =>   A^5 = ( 122  121 )
                                  ( 121  122 )

Long-run behaviour of a state matrix:

  M = ( 0.8  0.3 )   eigenvalues 1 and 0.5
      ( 0.2  0.7 )   lambda = 1 -> (3,2),  lambda = 0.5 -> (-1,1)

  Write x0 = a(3,2) + b(-1,1).  Then

     M^k x0 = a * 1^k * (3,2) + b * 0.5^k * (-1,1)

  The second term dies, so every start drifts to the (3,2) line:
  normalised to a probability vector, (0.6, 0.4).

annotations.text: The order of the columns of P must match the order of the eigenvalues in D. Swap one and the identity A = PDP^-1 breaks.
Every interior P^-1 P collapses to the identity, which is the entire trick: only the outermost P and P^-1 survive.
Expanding the start state in the eigenbasis is what makes the k-th step a sum of pure scalings, each with its own lambda^k.

checkpoint.prompt: Using $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ with $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$, compute $A^3$ explicitly and explain why the interior factors of the product cancel.
checkpoint.explain: Writing $A^3 = PDP^{-1}PDP^{-1}PDP^{-1}$, each interior $P^{-1}P$ is the identity, leaving $PD^3P^{-1}$ with $D^3 = \operatorname{diag}(27,1)$. That gives entries $(27+1)/2 = 14$ on the diagonal and $(27-1)/2 = 13$ off it. Multiplying $A$ by itself three times gives the same matrix, of course - the point is that the eigen-formula costs one cube instead of $k-1$ matrix products, and it keeps working when $k$ is left as a symbol.

guided-computation.prompt: For $B = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, complete the characteristic polynomial and its roots. Give plain integers, larger eigenvalue first.
guided-computation.explain: $\det(B - \lambda I) = (4-\lambda)(3-\lambda) - 2 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda-5)(\lambda-2)$. The coefficient of $\lambda$ is minus the trace and the constant is the determinant, so $5+2 = 7$ and $5 \times 2 = 10$ both check out. The commonest slip is dropping the $-2$ from the off-diagonal product, which would leave the roots $4$ and $3$ - the diagonal entries, which are the eigenvalues only for a triangular matrix.

guided-computation.prompt: Still with $B = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, evaluate each quantity. Give a single integer for each step.
guided-computation.explain: The determinant vanishes exactly at the eigenvalues, which is the whole content of the characteristic equation: $B - 5I$ and $B - 2I$ are singular, while $B - 3I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-2 \neq 0$ and so kills nothing but the zero vector. The rank of $B - 5I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ is $1$ because its rows are proportional, leaving a one-dimensional eigenspace - the drop in rank, not the drop to zero, is what counts how many eigenvectors you get.

guided-computation.prompt: Find both eigenvalues of $H = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & -2 \\ -2 & 9 \end{pmatrix}$ and a basis eigenvector for each. Verify one of your eigenpairs by computing $Hv$ directly, and say what is special about the angle between the two eigenvectors.
guided-computation.answer: lambda = 5 with v = (2,1); lambda = 10 with w = (-1,2). H(2,1) = (10,5) = 5(2,1). The eigenvectors are orthogonal: (2,1).(-1,2) = 0.
guided-computation.explain: $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 15\lambda + 50$ gives $\lambda = 5, 10$. For $\lambda = 5$, $(H-5I)v = 0$ reads $x - 2y = 0$, so $v = (2,1)$ and indeed $Hv = (12-2, -4+9) = (10,5) = 5v$; for $\lambda = 10$ the equation is $-4x - 2y = 0$, giving $w = (-1,2)$. Their dot product is $-2 + 2 = 0$: $H$ is symmetric, and a symmetric matrix always has orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues - a structural fact, not a coincidence of these numbers.

guided-computation.prompt: Arrange these steps into the standard procedure for finding all eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a square matrix $A$.
fragments: Form $A - \lambda I$ by subtracting $\lambda$ from each diagonal entry.
Compute $p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$ and set it equal to zero.
Solve the characteristic equation for its roots $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots$, recording the multiplicity of each root.
For one fixed root $\lambda_i$, substitute it back and row-reduce $A - \lambda_i I$.
Read off a basis of the null space of $A - \lambda_i I$; those vectors span the eigenspace $E_{\lambda_i}$.
Repeat for every remaining root, then check each pair against $Av = \lambda v$.
guided-computation.explain: The eigenvalues must be found before any eigenvector can be, because the system $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$ has no content until $\lambda$ is a specific number - with $\lambda$ still symbolic, row reduction would divide by expressions that may be zero. Note also that the eigenvectors are read off as a null-space **basis**, one substitution at a time, which is why a repeated root is handled at exactly the same point in the procedure as a simple one.

eigenstructure.prompt: Let $C = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, whose characteristic polynomial factors as $-(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)$. Find a basis eigenvector for $\lambda = 3$ by row-reducing $C - 3I$, confirm your vector satisfies $Cv = 3v$, and state $\dim E_3$ with a justification from the rank.
eigenstructure.explain: $C - 3I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ row-reduces to two independent rows, so its rank is $2$ and $\dim E_3 = 3 - 2 = 1$; solving leaves $z$ free with $x = -z$ and $y = z$, hence $v = (-1,1,1)$. The check $Cv = (-4+1, 2+1, 2+1) = (-3,3,3) = 3v$ is worth doing every time, because a sign error inside the row reduction produces a plausible-looking vector that fails it at once. A simple root can never give more than a one-dimensional eigenspace, so a two-dimensional answer here would be a signal that you had reduced the wrong matrix.

eigenstructure.prompt: Compare $N = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ with $M = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$, whose characteristic polynomial is $-(\lambda-6)(\lambda-4)^2$. For the repeated eigenvalue of each matrix give the algebraic multiplicity, the rank of $A - \lambda I$ and the geometric multiplicity, then say which matrix is defective and why a repeated root alone does not decide it.
eigenstructure.answer: N: lambda = 2 has algebraic multiplicity 2, rank(N-2I) = 2, geometric multiplicity 1, so N is defective. M: lambda = 4 has algebraic multiplicity 2, rank(M-4I) = 1, geometric multiplicity 2, so M is not defective. A repeated root only bounds the geometric multiplicity from above; the rank decides it.
eigenstructure.explain: Both matrices have a double root, yet they behave oppositely: $N - 2I$ keeps rank $2$, so $\dim E_2 = 1$ and $N$ is defective, while the rows of $M - 4I$ are all multiples of $(1,-1,-1)$, giving rank $1$, $\dim E_4 = 2$ and no defect. This is the point of keeping the two counts separate - the polynomial can only promise $\text{geometric} \le \text{algebraic}$, and only the rank of $A - \lambda I$ reports how many independent directions actually exist. Concluding 'repeated root, therefore not diagonalisable' is the standard error, and $M$ is the counterexample.

eigenstructure.prompt: The projection matrix $Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1/2 \\ 1/2 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1$ and $0$. Explain what each eigenvalue means geometrically for this map, why $\lambda = 0$ is a legitimate eigenvalue while $v = 0$ is not a legitimate eigenvector, and what an eigenvalue of $0$ tells you about invertibility.
eigenstructure.explain: $Q$ projects the plane onto the line through $(1,1)$: vectors already on that line are fixed, giving $\lambda = 1$, and vectors along $(1,-1)$ are flattened to the origin, giving $\lambda = 0$ with $E_0 = \operatorname{span}\{(1,-1)\}$. The eigenvalue $0$ is both legal and informative - it says $A$ has a non-trivial null space, hence $\det A = 0$ and $A$ is not invertible - whereas admitting $v = 0$ would be fatal, since $A0 = \lambda 0$ holds for every $\lambda$ and every scalar would become an eigenvalue. Confusing the harmless zero eigenvalue with the forbidden zero eigenvector is the usual muddle here.

eigenstructure.prompt: Let $A$ be square with eigenpairs $(\lambda_1, v_1)$ and $(\lambda_2, v_2)$ where $\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2$. Prove that $v_1$ and $v_2$ are linearly independent. Start from $c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 = 0$, apply $A$ to it, and eliminate one term.
eigenstructure.explain: Apply $A$ to $c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 = 0$ to get $c_1\lambda_1v_1 + c_2\lambda_2v_2 = 0$, then subtract $\lambda_2$ times the original relation: the $v_2$ term cancels and $c_1(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)v_1 = 0$ remains. Since $\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2$ and $v_1 \neq 0$, this forces $c_1 = 0$, and then $c_2v_2 = 0$ forces $c_2 = 0$. Both hypotheses do real work - distinctness makes the scalar factor non-zero, and the definition's insistence that an eigenvector is non-zero is what stops the argument collapsing. This result is exactly why $n$ distinct eigenvalues guarantee a full eigenbasis.

diagonalisation-workshop.prompt: Diagonalise $B = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$: give $P$, $D$ and $P^{-1}$ explicitly, say why $P$ is invertible, and use $B^3 = PD^3P^{-1}$ to compute $B^3$ as a matrix of integers.
diagonalisation-workshop.explain: The eigenpairs are $5$ with $(1,1)$ and $2$ with $(1,-2)$, so $P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $D = \operatorname{diag}(5,2)$; $P$ is invertible because its columns are eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues and hence independent, giving $\det P = -3 \neq 0$. With $D^3 = \operatorname{diag}(125, 8)$ the product $PD^3P^{-1}$ evaluates to $\begin{pmatrix} 86 & 39 \\ 78 & 47 \end{pmatrix}$, whose trace $133 = 125 + 8$ is a free check. Listing $D$ in an order that does not match the columns of $P$ is the classic wrecking move, and it shows up immediately as a wrong $B^3$.

diagonalisation-workshop.prompt: Suppose $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal. Prove by induction on $k \ge 1$ that $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$, and state what $D^k$ is in terms of the eigenvalues. Then explain in one sentence why this makes the behaviour of $A^k$ for large $k$ depend on the eigenvalue of largest absolute value.
diagonalisation-workshop.explain: The base case $k=1$ is the hypothesis itself; assuming $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$, we get $A^{k+1} = A^kA = PD^kP^{-1}PDP^{-1} = PD^kDP^{-1} = PD^{k+1}P^{-1}$, the single $P^{-1}P$ in the middle collapsing to $I$. Because $D$ is diagonal, $D^k = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^k, \ldots, \lambda_n^k)$ - diagonal matrices raise entrywise, which is precisely why the change of basis is worth making. For large $k$ the largest $|\lambda_i|$ dominates the others in ratio, so after rescaling $A^kx$ aligns with that eigenvector; note the proof never assumes the $\lambda_i$ are distinct, only that some diagonalisation exists.

diagonalisation-workshop.prompt: A population moves between two towns each year according to $M = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues are $1$ and $0.5$ with eigenvectors $(3,2)$ and $(-1,1)$. Starting from $x_0 = (1,0)$, write $x_0$ in the eigenbasis, give a closed form for $x_k = M^kx_0$, and state the limiting distribution with a reason drawn from the eigenvalues.
diagonalisation-workshop.explain: Solving $a(3,2) + b(-1,1) = (1,0)$ gives $a = 1/5$ and $b = -2/5$, so $x_k = \tfrac{1}{5}(3,2) - \tfrac{2}{5}(0.5)^k(-1,1)$; the second term decays geometrically while the first is untouched because $1^k = 1$, leaving the steady state $(0.6, 0.4)$. The eigenvalue $1$ is what makes a limit exist at all - it is forced here because each column of $M$ sums to $1$, so no population is created or destroyed - and the size of the subdominant eigenvalue $0.5$ sets the speed of convergence, halving the error each year. Iterating the matrix numerically would produce the same numbers but would explain neither the limit nor the rate.

exam.prompt: A vector $v$ is an **eigenvector** of the square matrix $A$ exactly when:
exam.explain: The exclusion belongs to the vector, not the scalar: $v = 0$ satisfies $Av = \lambda v$ for every $\lambda$ and would make the definition vacuous, while $\lambda = 0$ is a genuine eigenvalue signalling a non-trivial null space. The third option describes only that $\lambda = 0$ case, and the fourth substitutes a vector into the characteristic equation, where a scalar is required.

exam.prompt: Which of these statements about an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ are true by definition or by theorem? Select all that apply.
choices: $A$ is diagonalisable if and only if it has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors
Having $n$ distinct eigenvalues is sufficient for diagonalisability
Having $n$ distinct eigenvalues is necessary for diagonalisability
The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue never exceeds its algebraic multiplicity
The eigenspace $E_\lambda$ is the null space of $A - \lambda I$
exam.explain: Diagonalisability is precisely the existence of an eigenbasis, and distinct eigenvalues force independence, so they are sufficient - but the identity matrix is already diagonal with one eigenvalue repeated $n$ times, which settles that they are not necessary. The multiplicity inequality and the description of $E_\lambda$ as $\operatorname{null}(A - \lambda I)$ are both standard, and together they say a matrix fails to be diagonalisable exactly when some eigenvalue is defective.

exam.prompt: For the shear $S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, fill in the four quantities. Give plain integers, and write `yes` or `no` for the last.
exam.template:
the only eigenvalue of S is ___
its algebraic multiplicity is ___
its geometric multiplicity is ___
is S diagonalisable? ___
exam.explain: $p(\lambda) = (1-\lambda)^2$ makes $\lambda = 1$ a double root, but $S - I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has rank $1$, so $\dim E_1 = 2 - 1 = 1$ and only the $x$-axis is fixed. With one independent eigenvector in a two-dimensional space there is no invertible $P$ of eigenvectors, so $S$ is not diagonalisable - the defect is visible geometrically as the shear sliding every line except one.

exam.prompt: Arrange these lines into a valid derivation of the characteristic equation from the eigenvalue equation.
fragments: Rewrite the right-hand side as $\lambda I v$, so that both sides are matrices acting on $v$.
So the matrix $A - \lambda I$ sends a non-zero vector to $0$, that is, it has a non-trivial null space.
A square matrix with a non-trivial null space is singular, so $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$.
Hence the eigenvalues of $A$ are exactly the roots of the polynomial $p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I)$.
exam.explain: Inserting $I$ is the step that makes the subtraction legal, since $A - \lambda$ is not defined - a matrix and a scalar cannot be subtracted. Everything after it is a chain of equivalences about singularity, and the requirement $v \neq 0$ carried down from the first line is exactly what forces the determinant to vanish rather than merely permitting it.

exam.prompt: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalues $3$ and $1$, so that $A^k$ has diagonal entries $(3^k+1)/2$ and off-diagonal entries $(3^k-1)/2$. Give each answer as a single integer.
exam.explain: With $3^2 = 9$, $3^3 = 27$ and $3^5 = 243$ the formula gives $5$, $13$ and $122$ directly, and the trace of $A^5$ is $122 + 122 = 244 = 3^5 + 1^5$. That last identity is not a coincidence: the trace of $A^k$ is always the sum of the $k$-th powers of the eigenvalues, because $A^k$ and $D^k$ are similar and similar matrices share a trace.

exam.prompt: Let $G = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$. Find its eigenvalues, compute $G^2$, and use the eigenvalues to explain the result. What kind of geometric transformation does $G$ perform?
exam.answer: Eigenvalues 5 and -5; G^2 = 25I. G is a reflection scaled by 5: it fixes the eigenline for +5 and flips the eigenline for -5, so applying it twice restores every direction.
exam.explain: $\operatorname{tr} G = 0$ and $\det G = -25$ give $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 25$, so $\lambda = \pm 5$, and squaring sends both to $25$: $G^2 = 25I$, as direct multiplication confirms. Geometrically $G$ scales by $5$ and reflects across the eigenline for $+5$ - the eigenline for $-5$ is turned through half a turn - so two applications undo the flip and leave a pure scaling by $25$. The eigenvalue view explains the identity in one line, whereas multiplying the matrices out only verifies it.

exam.prompt: Let $R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, the quarter-turn anticlockwise. Compute its characteristic polynomial and show it has no real roots. Explain geometrically why that had to happen, and say what changes if complex scalars are allowed.
exam.answer: p(lambda) = lambda^2 + 1, whose discriminant is negative, so there is no real eigenvalue; over the complex numbers the eigenvalues are i and -i. Geometrically a quarter turn maps no real line to itself, so no real vector can satisfy Rv = lambda v.
exam.explain: $\operatorname{tr} R = 0$ and $\det R = 1$ give $p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 + 1$, with no real root. That is exactly what the geometry demands: an eigenvector spans a line the map sends back to itself, and a rotation by $90^\circ$ moves every line in the plane, so there is nothing for a real eigenvalue to describe. Over $\mathbb{C}$ the roots are $\pm i$ and $R$ is diagonalisable there - failing to be diagonalisable over $\mathbb{R}$ for want of roots is a different failure from being defective, where the roots exist but the eigenvectors run short.

exam.prompt: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix. Prove that $A$ is invertible if and only if $0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$. Then prove that if $Av = \lambda v$ with $v \neq 0$ and $A$ is invertible, then $A^{-1}v = \lambda^{-1}v$, and say why the assumption of invertibility is needed for that second claim to make sense.
exam.explain: $0$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $Av = 0$ for some $v \neq 0$, that is, when the null space is non-trivial, which for a square matrix is equivalent to $\det A = 0$ and so to non-invertibility; running that chain in both directions is the whole proof. For the second part, multiply $Av = \lambda v$ by $A^{-1}$ to get $v = \lambda A^{-1}v$, then divide by $\lambda$ - legal precisely because invertibility has already ruled out $\lambda = 0$. So $A$ and $A^{-1}$ share eigenvectors while their eigenvalues are reciprocals, which is why $A^{-1}$ magnifies exactly the directions $A$ shrinks.

exam.prompt: A student writes: "Every $n \times n$ matrix has $n$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, so every matrix has $n$ eigenvectors and is therefore diagonalisable." Identify the exact step that fails, name a $2 \times 2$ counterexample, and explain what diagonalisability really requires in terms of the two multiplicities.
exam.explain: The failure is the leap from roots to independent eigenvectors: the characteristic polynomial counts algebraic multiplicity, but the columns of $P$ must be geometrically independent, and $\dim E_\lambda = n - \operatorname{rank}(A - \lambda I)$ can fall short. The shear $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has $\lambda = 1$ twice yet only the single eigenline $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}$, so no eigenbasis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ exists. Diagonalisability requires geometric multiplicity to equal algebraic multiplicity for **every** eigenvalue; one defective eigenvalue is enough to sink the whole matrix.
